title: From keys to indexes: the idea of hashing
why: Everything else in this guide depends on one trick: converting a key into an array position. Start here.
objectives: Explain why searching a plain array or list is slow, and how an index fixes that
Describe what a hash function does and which properties it needs
Compute h(k) = k mod m by hand and spot a collision

quiz.q: Student IDs go up to 10<sup>9</sup>, but only 5,000 students are enrolled. Why is using the ID directly as an array index a bad idea?
options: The array would need about a billion slots, almost all of them empty
Array indexes cannot be numbers that large
It makes lookup slower than a linked list
quiz.explain: Direct addressing works, but the array must cover the whole range of possible keys, not just the keys you have. A billion slots to store 5,000 students wastes memory. Hashing squeezes the huge key range into a small array.

quiz.q: A good hash function maps every distinct key to a distinct index.
quiz.explain: False. When the key space is bigger than the array, the pigeonhole principle forces some keys to share an index. Those shared indexes are called collisions, and every hash table needs a plan for them (topic 2).

quiz.q: Which property must a hash function have for lookup to work at all?
options: It returns the same index every time for the same key
It returns a random index each call
It returns indexes in sorted key order
It never returns the same index twice
quiz.explain: We store a key at h(k) and later search at h(k). If the function gave a different answer the second time, we would look in the wrong place. Determinism is non-negotiable.

quiz.q: Table size m = 7 and h(k) = k mod 7. Which pair of keys collides?
quiz.explain: 10 mod 7 = 3 and 31 mod 7 = 3 (since 31 = 4·7 + 3). The others land on 3 & 4, 4 & 2, and 3 & 2, so they do not collide.

quiz.q: Select all properties that make a hash function good.
options: Spreads keys evenly over the indexes
Keeps the keys in sorted order
quiz.explain: Fast, even spread and deterministic are what you want. Sorted order is not a goal; a hash table deliberately scatters keys, which is why it cannot give you “the next largest key” cheaply.

task.title: Hash it by hand
task.prompt: Fill in the blanks. Use h(k) = k mod 7 for the calculation.
task.text: A hash function maps a [[key]] to an [[index|array index|bucket]] in an array of size m. Two different keys that map to the same index are called a [[collision]]. With h(k) = k mod 7, the key 52 goes to index [[3]].

cards.front: What does a hash function do?
cards.back: Maps a key (of any size) to an array index in 0 … m−1, deterministically.

cards.front: Why is a plain unsorted array slow for lookup?
cards.back: You must scan it element by element: O(n) in the worst case.
Two different keys that the hash function maps to the same index.
The set of possible keys is much larger than the array, so by the pigeonhole principle some keys must share an index.

cards.front: Compute 31 mod 7 and say what it means as a hash.
cards.back: 31 = 4·7 + 3, so h(31) = 3. The key 31 is stored in slot 3.
